title: Trees: Lowest Common Ancestor
oneLiner: Each call reports back whether it found p or q below it; the first node that hears "found" from both sides is the answer.
keyTakeaway: Recurse into both children. A call returns the node itself if it IS p or q, otherwise whatever non-null result came back from its children. If BOTH children return something, p and q are on different sides and this node is the lowest common ancestor. One post-order pass, O(n), no parent pointers needed.
explanation:
Given a binary tree (a general one, not a BST, so values tell you nothing about direction) and two values p and q that are both in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree. A node counts as its own ancestor, so if p sits below q, the answer is q. Values are distinct, and the tree comes from a level-order array where null marks a missing child.

Let each recursive call answer one question about its subtree: "did you find p or q down there, and if so, which node should I report?" The rules are short. A null node reports nothing. A node that IS p or q reports itself immediately, without looking further down. Otherwise ask both children. If both report something, p is on one side and q on the other, so this node is where their paths split: report this node. If only one side reports something, pass that up unchanged. At the root, whatever comes back is the answer.

Why is it fine to stop at p without searching under it? If q is below p, then p is the answer, and nothing above will ever see a second report from another side, so p's report travels all the way up. If q is elsewhere, some ancestor will receive p from one side and q from the other. Either way the right node surfaces. Each node is visited at most once: O(n) time, O(h) stack.

Common follow-ups: in a BST you don't need this at all -- walk down from the root, going left while both values are smaller and right while both are larger; the first node between them is the LCA, in O(h). If nodes have parent pointers, it becomes "intersection of two linked lists": walk both up. And if p or q might be missing, this version can return the wrong node; you then need to count how many of the two were actually found.

starterCode.python:
def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):

        # Otherwise recurse left and right. If both sides return a node,

        return None

    lca = find(root)
    return -1 if lca is None else lca.val

visualizationSteps.message: Find the LCA of p = 6 and q = 4. Each call reports p or q if it finds one below it, or nothing (null).
Node 6 is p. Report it upward right away -- no need to look below it.
Node 7: neither side found p or q. Report null.
Node 4 is q. Report it upward right away -- no need to look below it.
Node 2: only the right side found something (4). Pass 4 up unchanged.
Node 5 hears 6 from the left and 4 from the right. p and q split here, so 5 is the LCA: report 5.
Node 0: neither side found p or q. Report null.
Node 8: neither side found p or q. Report null.
Node 1: neither side found p or q. Report null.
Node 3: only the left side found something (5). Pass 5 up unchanged.
The root returns 5: that is the lowest common ancestor of 6 and 4.

recognitionSignals: "Lowest common ancestor", "first shared manager of two employees", or "where do these two paths in a hierarchy meet?"
You need information from BOTH subtrees before you can decide at a node -- a bottom-up (post-order) DFS that returns something to the parent.
gotchas: Using the BST shortcut (compare values to decide left or right) on a general binary tree: values don't tell you which side anything is on here.
Forgetting that a node can be its own ancestor: when q is in p's subtree the answer is p, which the early "node is p or q, return it" check handles for free.
This version assumes both p and q exist. If one might be missing, it would wrongly return the one it found, so count the matches before trusting the result.
confusableWith: Binary Search Trees: Search uses the BST ordering to pick a direction; the BST version of LCA does the same, but a general binary tree has no ordering, so you must search both sides.
Trees: Diameter of a Binary Tree (this track) has the same post-order "children report to the parent" shape, but returns a height instead of a found node.

complexity.note: Each node is visited at most once in the post-order search; the recursion stack is the tree's height, O(n) in the worst (skewed) case.
